newsitem.title: USA: Republicans say deal on U.S. budget, tax cuts near.
newsitem.headline: Republicans say deal on U.S. budget, tax cuts near.

text.p: Republican leaders said on Sunday a deal on legislation to cut taxes and balance the budget over five years was virtually complete, although the White House warned some thorny issues still remained.
After a day of internal meetings and phone calls with administration officials, House Speaker Newt Gingrich said "virtually nothing" was left to resolve.
The White House, however, said agreement was still needed on some key issues.

"There are still important issues such as who gets the tax cut and children's health care that are unresolved and critical to a sound balanced budget agreement," Gene Sperling, White House economic adviser, said in a telephone interview.
"Nothing is agreed to on the tax package until everything is agreed to," he reiterated.

White House officials had been expected at Capitol Hill to resume face-to-face talks with Republicans on Sunday evening but did not show up. Lawmakers called it a scheduling misunderstanding and said they expected to have final budget legislation completed by Monday night.
Congressional aides said both sides had made important concessions on contentious tax issues that had held up an agreement.

Republicans were expected to drop a provision that would not tax investment profits attributable to inflation. President Bill Clinton has strongly opposed that capital gains "indexing" plan, contending it could worsen the budget deficit in later years.

"I'll have a chance next year with another tax package to maybe pick up those pieces that get lost behind in this one," House Majority Leader Dick Armey, a Texas Republican, said on ABC's "This Week."
An expected White House compromise on the capital gains tax would allow cutting the top rate to 20 percent from 28 percent, congressional sources said.
The White House was expected to go along with Republican demands to let upper-middle income taxpayers claim a $500 per child tax credit by placing the income ceiling at $110,000.

Republicans showed willingness to expand the child credit to more low-income workers, which the White House has sought. But they want the administration to agree to reform a tax subsidy for the working poor, the Earned Income Tax Credit.

Proposals to make affluent seniors pay higher Medicare premiums, gradually raise the programme eligibility age to 67 from 65 and institute a $5 co-payment for home health visits would not be included in the final deal, aides said.
The legislation will call for a commission to suggest long-term Medicare reforms.

The White House showed a willingness for a higher education tax package amounting closer to $30 billion over five years than the $35 billion Clinton has insisted on. But the package was expected to include the president's programme for a $1,500 HOPE scholarship tax credit for higher education costs and a 20 percent tuition tax deduction.
Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, said the final tax bill would made progress on his priority issue of expanding Individual Retirement Accounts.
"I believe (that) in the final tax bill we'll make good progress on IRAs," he said. "I think we'll have everything buttoned down tomorrow night."
